title: The Edge: CDNs, HTTP Caching, and DNS
intro: The fastest request is one that never reaches your servers. A content delivery network (CDN) keeps copies of your responses in hundreds of locations near users. Whether it can depends almost entirely on a few HTTP headers you control.

steps.prompt: Check how a static asset is being cached: fetch only the headers of https://shop.example.com/static/app.8c7e5a.js and show the caching ones.
steps.fake_output:
cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
etag: "8c7e5a667f1b"
age: 86212
x-cache: Hit from cloudfront
steps.explanation: Served from the CDN (a hit), cached for a year, and the copy is about a day old.
steps.why: 'x-cache: Hit' means your servers never saw this request. 'Age' is how long the edge has held it. A year-long max-age is safe here only because of the next step.

steps.prompt:
The file is cached for a year. How do you ship a new version of app.js to users?
  a) Wait a year
  b) Put a hash of the content in the filename (app.8c7e5a.js), so a new version is a new URL
  c) Purge the whole CDN on every deploy
  d) Set max-age to 0 on everything
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
app.8c7e5a.js -> cached for ever (the content at this URL never changes)
new build     -> app.f41d09.js, referenced from the HTML
index.html    -> short cache (or no-cache), so users pick up the new file names quickly
steps.hint: If the URL changes whenever the content changes, the old cached copy is never wrong.
steps.why: This turns cache invalidation, a hard problem, into a non-problem: cached files are immutable, and only the small HTML page that names them needs to stay fresh. Purging the CDN works but is slow, rate-limited, and easy to forget.

steps.prompt: Now check the product API response: fetch only the headers of https://shop.example.com/api/products/42 and show the caching ones.
steps.fake_output:
cache-control: private, no-store
x-cache: Miss from cloudfront
steps.explanation: private, no-store: neither the CDN nor the browser may cache it, so every request reaches your servers.
steps.why: 'private, no-store' is right for personal data (a user's cart, their account). For public data like a product page, it throws away the cheapest scaling you have. 'public, max-age=60' would let the CDN absorb almost all of that traffic, at the cost of prices being up to a minute stale.

steps.prompt:
Product details change rarely, but the same URL is requested 5,000 times a second. Which header value fits?
  a) cache-control: private, no-store
  b) cache-control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300
  c) cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
  d) No cache-control header at all
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
s-maxage=60                  the CDN keeps it 60 seconds -> your servers see ~1 request/minute per edge instead of 5,000/second
stale-while-revalidate=300   after 60s the CDN serves the old copy at once and refreshes it in the background
steps.hint: You want the CDN to cache it briefly, and never make users wait while it refreshes.
steps.explanation: A short shared cache with stale-while-revalidate.
steps.why: s-maxage applies to shared caches (the CDN) only, so browsers still check back. stale-while-revalidate means nobody waits for the refresh, and it prevents a stampede when the entry expires. A year-long cache would be wrong: unlike the hashed JS file, this URL's content changes.

steps.prompt: How do users reach the nearest edge in the first place? Resolve shop.example.com.
steps.explanation: The name is an alias for the CDN, which answers with addresses near whoever asked.
steps.why: CDNs steer users with DNS and anycast: the same name resolves to a nearby location for each user. DNS answers are cached too (the TTL), which is why DNS-based failover is never instant: a 300-second TTL means some users keep the old address for 5 minutes.
